input:
## Current use

This energy assessment presents the current energy position of a dairy plant and considers the scope for reducing its energy consumption. The plant uses 1059 MWh of electricity per year, and of the various demands placed on the electrical supply, refrigeration is responsible for the largest share. This pattern will be familiar to anyone acquainted with dairy operations, since milk and dairy products have to be kept cold from the moment the milk arrives at the site until the moment the finished product leaves it. Nevertheless, the dominance of refrigeration in the electricity total does mean that it is the natural focus of any assessment of this kind, and it is with refrigeration that the detailed discussion below begins.

In addition to refrigeration itself, the assessment also considers the steam system, which serves the heating duties of the plant, and it concludes with a recommendation concerning a heat-recovery retrofit that has been proposed for the site. Before turning to the detail, it should be said that the purpose of this assessment is to establish the current position on the basis of the records that are available, and to evaluate the proposed retrofit on the figures that those records support.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the dairy plant serves a wide range of duties. Raw milk has to be cooled on arrival and held cold in storage before it is processed, and finished products such as yoghurt and cream have to be cooled after processing and held in cold stores until they are dispatched. Refrigeration is also involved in the cooling of process streams at various points in the production sequence. It is important to appreciate that several of these loads are effectively continuous: cold stores lose cold to their surroundings at all hours, and milk arrives at the site throughout the day, so that the refrigeration plant is called upon to operate for extended periods rather than only during the hours of production.

It follows from this that the refrigeration system is not merely the largest single consumer of electricity at the plant but also one of the most continuously operating systems on the site. The heat that the refrigeration plant rejects as it works is, in principle, available for recovery, and it is this rejected heat that the proposed retrofit is designed to capture. However, the value of capturing it depends on there being a demand for heat at the times when the refrigeration plant is rejecting it, and this question of timing is one that will recur in the recommendation.

## Steam

Steam is used at the dairy plant for the heating duties associated with processing, including the heating of product streams and the cleaning of equipment and pipework, which in a dairy is a substantial and recurring duty. It is, however, of the utmost importance to note a significant limitation affecting the steam figures used in this assessment: the steam figures are taken from one winter month, and they therefore reflect the operating conditions of the plant during the coldest part of the year rather than providing an even picture across all of the seasons. The recommendation that follows will accordingly flag the steam figures as seasonal, and any conclusions that rest upon them should be treated with appropriate caution.

Because cleaning is such a large part of the steam demand in a dairy, and because cleaning takes place at particular points in the production cycle, the steam demand of the plant is far from steady over the course of a day. This has a bearing on the heat-recovery question, since recovered heat can only displace steam that would otherwise have been raised at that moment, and steam that is demanded in short peaks cannot always be matched by heat that is rejected on a different pattern.

## Recommendation

The recommendation arising from this assessment concerns the proposed heat-recovery retrofit. The retrofit is projected to save 17% of the plant's electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 180 MWh per year, and its capital cost is $877k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving amounts to $21604, and the derived simple payback works out at 40.6 years. It is only fair to acknowledge that this is a very long payback period, and it means that the retrofit, considered purely as a means of saving electricity, repays its capital cost only over a timescale that extends far beyond the horizon over which such projects are normally assessed. As flagged above, the steam figures are seasonal, having been drawn from one winter month, and this qualification should be borne in mind in connection with any part of the case that depends on steam. The assessment therefore presents the retrofit figures as they stand, notes the length of the payback, and draws attention to the seasonal nature of the steam evidence on which parts of the assessment rest.

It is also worth observing that the general pattern described in this assessment, with refrigeration dominating the electricity consumption of the site, is one that is encountered again and again in the dairy industry, and indeed in food processing more generally, wherever a product has to be kept cold continuously from its arrival in raw form through to its departure as a finished article. The cold chain admits of no real interruption, and the electricity that it consumes is therefore one of the least discretionary items in the entire cost base of a plant of this kind. This is part of the reason why energy assessments of dairy plants so often return to the refrigeration system when they are looking for savings, since it is at one and the same time the largest load and the load that is most continuously present.

A related consideration is the extent to which the different energy systems of the plant interact with one another. Electricity and steam are sometimes discussed as though they were separate subjects, but in a plant of this kind they are closely connected: the refrigeration system consumes electricity and produces rejected heat, while the steam system consumes fuel in order to produce heat, and it is precisely at the junction between these two systems that the proposed retrofit is intended to operate. An improvement in one system can therefore have consequences in the other, and it is important that these consequences are thought through as a whole rather than evaluated in isolation, since a saving that appears in one account may be partly offset by an increase that appears in the other, and only a view of the plant as a complete system will reveal whether this is happening.

## Current use

The dairy plant uses 1059 MWh of electricity per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share. The structure of the assessment follows from that single fact: the refrigeration section describes where the electricity goes, the steam section describes the heating system against which any recovered heat would be credited, and the recommendation evaluates a heat-recovery retrofit whose case rests on the relationship between the two systems.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the plant covers the cooling of raw milk on arrival, its storage before processing, the cooling of products after processing, and the cold storage of finished products until dispatch. Two properties of this load govern its place in the assessment. The first is its size relative to the other electrical demands of the site: it exceeds each of them, so a given fractional saving in refrigeration is worth more than the same fraction anywhere else in the electricity account. The second is its continuity. Cold stores lose cold to their surroundings at all hours, and milk arrives across the day, so the refrigeration plant runs far beyond the hours of production. A continuous refrigeration load rejects heat continuously, including at night and at weekends, and that timing decides how much of the rejected heat can be used: recovered heat has value only where a heating demand exists at the moment of recovery, and a dairy's heating demands are concentrated in processing and cleaning periods rather than spread evenly across the week.

The refrigeration system is therefore both the largest consumer of electricity at the plant and the source of the heat the proposed retrofit would recover. Those two statements are not independent. The projected electricity saving from heat recovery arises because heat recovered from refrigeration displaces electric or steam heating elsewhere; the size of the refrigeration load sets the quantity of heat available, and its timing sets the share of that heat for which a demand exists.

## Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the plant: the heating of product streams during processing and the cleaning of equipment and pipework, which in a dairy is a large and recurring duty. Steam demand is not steady. Cleaning takes place at set points in the production cycle, so demand arrives in peaks, and recovered heat can displace only the steam that would otherwise be raised at the moment the heat becomes available.

The steam figures in this assessment are from one winter month and are seasonal. They record the plant in the coldest part of the year, when incoming water is at its coldest and the heating component of processing is at its largest. A steam total built on a winter month overstates the annual steam demand, and a saving calculated by displacement against that total inherits the overstatement in the same proportion. The figures are used in this assessment because they are the records available; the qualification is stated here and carried into the recommendation, and it applies to every conclusion that rests on the steam side of the plant's energy balance.

## Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 17% of electricity use, a derived saving of 180 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $877k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $21604 and the derived simple payback is 40.6 years.

The payback is the finding of this assessment. That payback means that the retrofit, judged on the stated electricity saving alone, returns its capital cost over a period far longer than the working life over which such equipment is normally assessed, and the case for the retrofit cannot be made on the energy figures as they stand. The projected saving is a projection, not a measurement, and it is stated as such; the seasonal character of the steam figures, flagged in the steam section, qualifies the steam side of the assessment but does not rescue the payback, which is computed from the annual electricity figures. The recommendation is therefore that the retrofit not be approved on the present case. A case could be reopened on different evidence: a measured refrigeration load profile across a full year, steam records for a full year in place of the single winter month, or a capital cost materially below the figure quoted. On the evidence in this assessment, the electricity saving is real in direction and insufficient in size, and the plant's energy attention is better spent first on the refrigeration load itself, whose size is the reason both the electricity total and the rejected-heat quantity are what they are.

The electricity total also sets the scale against which every recommendation in this assessment must be judged. A measure that saves a small fraction of a small load is a small measure, whatever its percentage, and the percentages quoted for individual systems can mislead a reader who does not hold the total in mind. Refrigeration's share of the total is the reason the retrofit was evaluated at all: a heat-recovery project attached to a minor load could not have produced even the saving projected here. The share is equally the reason the assessment ends where it does, because the same dominance that makes refrigeration the obvious place to look for savings also means that the load itself, rather than the recovery of its rejected heat, is the quantity that most deserves the plant's attention.

Within the refrigeration load, the duties differ in how they can be changed. The cooling of incoming milk is fixed in quantity by the volume and temperature of the milk itself, and no efficiency measure alters the heat that must be removed from it; only the efficiency of the plant that removes it can change. Cold storage, by contrast, contains an element that better insulation, better door discipline, and better control of infiltration can genuinely reduce, because part of that load is heat leaking into a space that is then expensively held cold. An assessment that treats the refrigeration total as one number cannot separate the part of the load that is intrinsic to the product from the part that is an artefact of the building and its operation, and the separation matters, because the two parts respond to different measures and different spending.

The steam system has its own bearing on the retrofit question that the payback figure alone does not capture. Recovered heat from refrigeration is available at the times the refrigeration plant runs, which is to say broadly and continuously; steam demand at the plant is concentrated at cleaning and at processing peaks. The mismatch does not appear in an annual balance, where the totals can be set against each other as if they were simultaneous, but it appears in operation, where heat recovered at a moment of no demand is heat wasted. A design that took the annual totals at face value would overstate the displacement the retrofit can achieve, and the overstatement would grow with the size of the installation. This is a further reason, beyond the payback, for treating the projected saving as an upper bound on what the retrofit would deliver.

The assessment closes on the state of the evidence rather than on the state of the plant. The plant's energy position, as far as the records show it, is ordinary for its type: a refrigeration-dominated electricity demand, a seasonal and peaky steam demand, and a proposed retrofit whose projected saving is too small against its cost. What is not ordinary is how much of the case rested on how little record: a single winter month of steam data asked to support annual conclusions, and a projected saving asked to support a capital decision. The plant can put both right cheaply, by metering and by keeping the records it already generates for a full year before the question is asked again. The next assessment of this plant should be able to argue from a year of evidence, and this one is written so that its conclusions can be replaced by that argument, point by point, when the evidence exists.
